implementation_notes: Rust encodes the actor's central rule in the type system: sending a value through a channel moves it, so the compiler rejects using it afterwards (the Rust book demonstrates the borrow-of-moved-value error), and the actor's state can live exclusively inside the task's frame - no Arc<Mutex<_>>, because the mailbox is the only way in. The classic structure is replaced by a spawned task or thread owning the state, a cloneable Sender as the address, and a bounded receiver for backpressure: tokio::sync::mpsc::channel(n) makes send await when full, and the documentation spells out the disconnection semantics that end the actor. Choose std::sync::mpsc for blocking threads and tokio (or actix/ractor) for async actors; frameworks add supervision, timers and named actors on top of the same shape.
pitfalls: An unbounded channel (tokio::sync::mpsc::unbounded_channel) removes backpressure and is the standard way a Rust actor turns into an OOM bug; prefer bounded senders with await.
When every Sender drops, recv returns None and the actor exits; holding a Sender inside the actor itself keeps it alive forever.
Blocking a tokio worker with std::thread::sleep or blocking I/O stalls the runtime; use spawn_blocking or a dedicated actor thread.
Cloning the Sender is how addresses multiply, so decide the public address type deliberately - exposing rx or the actor struct breaks single-writer ownership.
